messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai was forty-one, a dancer with a small contemporary company in a Midwestern city, but his body still remembered the evening in the war zone seven years ago. He had been a relief worker then, part of a medical convoy shelled on a dirt road at dusk. Smoke poured from the vehicle ahead—burnt rubber and diesel, mixed with the sharp reek of ethanol from spilled medical supplies. He had frozen, crouched behind a wall, while a colleague bled out in the open. He did not go to her. That moment, the smell, the time of day—they became the coordinates of a shame he carried like a second spine.

Now, the same hour triggered him almost without fail. When the sun slanted through the rehearsal room windows in late afternoon, Kai’s chest would tighten, and he would catch a phantom scent—burnt plastic, alcohol—even if the air was clean. The triggers worked so fast they felt like a switch. A whiff of whiskey on a patron after a show, or the acrid smell of a smoke machine during dress rehearsal, and the memory would arrive without warning, reliving the moment: the dirt grit under his palms, the heat, the silence after the blast, the certainty that he had done the wrong thing. He felt it happen *now*, not then.

Kai had come to believe that his actions that evening revealed something fundamental: he had violated his own deepest values, had let a person die because he was a coward. He told himself that a better person would have run into the open, but he had stayed frozen. This appraisal—that he was a lousy coper—colored everything. He could not trust his own instincts. When the memory intruded, it brought a wave of shame that confirmed his self-condemnation. And because he was certain he could not rely on himself, he became hypervigilant, scanning his environment for any possible trigger—a strange burnt smell, the time of day, the sound of a distant siren—so that he would not be caught off guard again. But this vigilance only made the triggers more frequent: his constant checking kept his trauma at the front of his mind, ready to be activated.

The loops tightened over months. He began to avoid evening performances, finding excuses to stay out of the rehearsal space when the light dropped. He stopped going to post-show gatherings where alcohol was present. At home, his wife would find him sitting rigidly on the couch at dusk, staring at nothing, and he could not explain why—only that the shame was too large to share. His career suffered; the artistic director complained he was unreliable. Kai was afraid that if he stopped avoiding, the memory would swallow him whole, that he would relive the moment again and again until he broke. But the avoidance wore him down, and his sense of being a bad coper deepened.

What finally brought him to my office was a mid-summer evening when a theater nearby caught fire. The burnt smell drifted through his apartment, and he spent four hours in a dissociated state, convinced he was back on that road, watching his colleague die. His wife found him on the bathroom floor, weeping with a shame so acute he could barely speak. He came to therapy because he was terrified of that happening again—and because somewhere, in a part of himself he barely trusted, he hoped that maybe he could still learn to rely on the person he had been before.
